reason: Pistillate flowers have a colour. The examples are correct.
Large or ample leaf sheaths. The size is meaningful.
Panicle colour is meaningful. Some examples describe the colour of the hairs (indument), which is still a colour of the panicle.
The operculum (lid) has a 2-D shape such as ovate.
A penicillate (brush-like) style is a standard term.
Capsules can be obovate.
A legume can be attenuate at its ends.
Secondary veins can be ascending or spreading, which is orientation.
Bud scales have a shape. Some examples describe the apex or margin, so a rule should send those to the sub-part.
Cells can be small. This is common in moss floras.
Valvate and imbricate describe how bud scales are arranged, which is a spatial pattern.
Glabrous is meaningful for this part, for example a corona. The examples are correct.
Teeth can be spreading.
The examples are about margins that are hyaline, and one is about trichomes. A rule would need to assign the quality to the margin, not the whole lamina, and to drop the trichome cases.
Bracts can be wide. Comparative statements such as 'broader than' may need a separate rule.
Ellipsoid is mapped to prolate. A nut can be ellipsoid.
Glabrous is meaningful. The examples include surface qualifiers (adaxially), which are acceptable.
The examples describe hairlike appendages or papillae on the seed, not a filiform seed. This is a wrong reading, and the quality belongs to the appendage.
Petals can overlap, as in an imbricate corolla.
Leaf sheaths can be chestnut brown, which is a red-brown colour.
A velvety indument on bracts is common.
Stamens can be persistent.
Lobes can be subcircular.
An ovary can be subcylindrical.
A palea can be winged. The keel wings are part of the palea.
The examples say 'straight hairs', so the quality belongs to the trichome and not the leaflet. The part is wrong.
A leaf apex can be cuspidate.
An indusium can be glandular. Some examples describe glands on the margin, which is fine.
Axes can be flexuous, which is sinuous.
An indusium can be continuous or interrupted.
A ligule can be leathery (coriaceous).
A connective can be narrow.
Auricles can be inconspicuous.
Pollinia can be ellipsoid.
Veins can have a colour. A few examples describe the leaf colour instead, so the annotation is not always clean.
Scale leaves and cataphylls can be persistent.
Lobes can be reflexed.
The examples are about stinging hairs, so this is a wrong reading. The disposition (stinging) belongs to the trichome, not the whole plant.
A receptacle can be small.
An androgynophore has a length.
The examples say the thecae are superposed. A rule would need to move the quality to the anther theca instead of the anther.
The examples are about heads or inflorescences placed one above the other. A rule would need to tell this arrangement of several inflorescences apart from the shape of one.
A capsule can be radially symmetric (actinomorphic).
A rachis can be hairy.
The examples are rhizome scales, which does not match the part label. Part and examples disagree, so the pair comes from a wrong reading.
A seed can be oblate (depressed-globose).
An ovary can be constricted, for example at its neck.
An ovary can be punctate (gland-dotted).
A pinnule can be auriculate.
A trichome can be sessile.
A flower can be odorless.
The examples give thickness, which is not the same as PATO depth. A rule would need to map 'thick' to a thickness term or confirm depth is the intended term.
Beak length is meaningful. One example is a distance from the beak tip, which is a measurement.
A bract can be firm in texture.
An apex can be acute or blunt, which is sharpness.
A spike can be ellipsoid.
A flower can be nocturnal.
An indusium can be horseshoe-shaped or pouch-forming, which is a concave shape.
An epidermis can be cobwebby (arachnose).
A bracteole can have parallel veins.
